Omitted or empty for proxy delivery means `["*"]`. No scheme, port, path, partial wildcard, IP literal, or local hostname. Destination checks also reject private and restricted resolved addresses. This scopes credential use, not all sandbox network access.

SecretName.description: A unique environment variable name within an org. The names a sandbox's env reserves are reserved (shell variables such as PATH, HOME, BASH_ENV, ENV and IFS, session and trust-store variables, and INSTABOX_ and SSH_ prefixes). A Secret saved under a name before it was reserved is not delivered: the machine's guest status names it.

SecretProxyStatus.description: Last node acknowledgement, not continuous health. Policies expire within 60 seconds unless renewed. Revocation is pending until applied or the previous lease expires. Already admitted streams may finish.

appliedRevision.description: Last revision acknowledged by the node.

SecretSelection.description: Proxy selection only. All includes current and future proxy Secrets in the sandbox's org. Explicit names resolve to stable IDs. An empty array selects none. Deleting and recreating a name does not restore an explicit grant. Null is rejected.

SecretUsage.description: This sandbox's HTTPS requests carrying the Secret's placeholder. requests had the real value injected; denied went to a host outside the Secret's hosts and were refused. Lags by up to a policy renewal and covers only hosts the proxy intercepts.

lastUsedAt.description: Last request with the value injected; denied requests do not move it.

SecretValue.description: UTF-8 text without NUL, at most 65536 bytes. Empty values are valid. Proxy values must also be valid HTTP header values without CR or LF.

lastUsedAt.description: Last browser use, or the last token refresh of a CLI session.

Snapshot.description: A saved copy of a sandbox (software and files). New sandboxes can be created from it. It belongs to its source sandbox's org: every member of the org sees, uses and deletes it.

dataSizeBytes.description: The logical size of the storage disk (`/data`) a sandbox created from it gets, not the bytes stored (the saved data is sparse and compressed); absent for system-files-only snapshots. Sandboxes created from it get at least this much storage.

defaultSpec.description: The size a sandbox created from this snapshot gets when the create names none: the caller's plan default for vCPUs and memory (`limits.machineSpec`, 4 vCPU / 8 GiB on api.instabox.sh), not the source sandbox's size, so a snapshot of a 2/4 box creates a 4/8 one unless the create passes `vcpus` and `memMiB`; plus the storage (`/data`) and system disk sizes the snapshot was saved with, which a created sandbox gets at least. Absent when its template is unknown.

exclusiveBytes.description: No longer computed; servers leave it out. (Was the stored bytes only this snapshot references.)

guestUser.description: The source sandbox's Linux user (`Machine.guestUser`), which a sandbox created from this snapshot keeps unless the create names another. `dev` for snapshots of sandboxes from older templates.

name.description: Unique among the org's live snapshots.

orgId.description: The org the snapshot belongs to (its source sandbox's).

publishedAt.description: When the visibility became community or official.

rootSizeBytes.description: The logical size of the system disk a sandbox created from it gets (its provisioned capacity), not the bytes stored: a snapshot is saved sparse and compressed.

sourceSnapshotSeq.description: The source sandbox's saved state (`storage.snapshotSeq`) this snapshot was taken from; 0 for a live snapshot of a sandbox that was never stopped.

status.description: `ready` can be used. A snapshot of a running sandbox is `pending` while it uploads (its sizes are the sandbox's until then), then `ready` or `failed`.

visibility.description: Who can create from the snapshot (docs/community-templates.md): `private` (the default, its org's members), `community` (every signed-in account) or `official` (listed next to the built-in templates). Absent on older servers: treat as private. Handlers do not set community or official yet.

StartMachineRequest.description: A body key that is none of these is refused with `400 unknown_field` (keys match case-insensitively) and nothing is started; an empty body or `{}` is valid.

host.description: Admin only: place the sandbox on this host. While `storage.synced` is false the sandbox can only start on its current host; another host gets `409 operation_conflict`.

memMiB.description: New memory (MiB) of the stopped sandbox, as `vcpus`; absent: its current size.

vault.description: False disables legacy Vault delivery without changing org Secret selections.

vcpus.description: Start a stopped paid sandbox at another of the workspace's `allowedSpecs`, as `PATCH` `vcpus`/`memMiB` then `start` would: with `memMiB`, one of them (alone: the one size with that many vCPUs). Absent: its current size. The size is stored before the start and the boot asks for it; read it from the sandbox's `spec` (the start Operation carries no request body). Its current size changes nothing; a running sandbox at another size is `409 operation_conflict` (stop it first), and so is a paused one (resume it, then stop it), as is a sandbox whose start is already active (naming it: only the same size, or none, joins that start); another size, or the free sandbox, is `400 spec_not_allowed`; 0 or a negative is `400 bad_request`.

StopMachineRequest.description: A body key that is none of these is refused with `400 unknown_field` (keys match case-insensitively) and nothing is stopped; an empty body or `{}` is valid.

timeoutSeconds.description: How long to wait for a clean shutdown before the sandbox is forced off.

Storage.description: The sandbox's storage (`/data`, where HOME lives).

snapshotSeq.description: Sequence number of the sandbox's latest saved state; absent before the first stop or pause.

synced.description: False while the latest state of a stopped or paused sandbox is still being saved: for a few seconds after a stop or pause, or longer if saving fails (it is retried). A snapshot waits until it is true.

SuspendMachineRequest.description: The optional body of `POST /v1/machines/{id}/suspend`, which takes no fields; any key is refused with `400 unknown_field`.

Template.description: A template version a sandbox can start from. Versions never change.

capabilities.description: `identity-reset`: its sandboxes can be snapshotted. `root-grow`: an admin can grow its sandboxes' sizes. `orca`: its sandboxes run an Orca runtime (`POST /v1/machines/{id}/orca-connections`). `activity`: it ships activity probes for its agents, so pausing when idle (`autoSuspendAfterSeconds`) sees them working; without it, terminal and CPU activity alone count.

creatable.description: Whether a create may name this template (`POST /v1/machines` `templateId`): false for a `hidden` one, which is refused with `400`. The org's plan may still refuse a creatable one (`403 template_not_allowed`; the free plan creates from agent-browser, android, omarchy or ci only). Absent on servers older than this field: use `!hidden`.

default.description: This is the version a create naming neither `templateId` nor `snapshotId` gets (the `latest` agent-browser). Absent on servers older than this field.

gpu.description: A GPU template: a create from it needs `gpu` (CreateMachineRequest), and a create with `gpu` takes only a GPU template. GPU sandboxes are for paid plans.

gpuTypes.description: On a GPU template, the GPU types a create from it may ask for. Absent on every other template.

hidden.description: This template is no longer offered for new sandboxes: a create naming it is refused. It is still listed so that sandboxes and snapshots built on it keep showing its size and capabilities.

kernel.description: The guest kernel this version runs, `sha256:<hex>`: every sandbox created from it is pinned to that kernel for its whole life (cold boots, snapshots, restores and moves never use another) and is placed only on hosts that have it. Absent: the host's default kernel (every template before this field).

latest.description: This is the version a create naming this `templateId` without a `templateVersion` gets: set on one creatable version per id. Absent on servers older than this field: the last listed version of the id, when it is creatable (a hidden one: none).

os.description: The guest OS of a template with a pool. Absent: Linux.

pool.description: The host pool every sandbox of this version runs in (e.g. `mac` for macOS); its `defaultSpec` and `sizes` are then the sizes such a sandbox gets, whatever the plan's sizes and vCPU limit. Absent: the default placement and the server's sandbox size.

preboot.description: New sandboxes of this template version start faster: they come from an already booted copy, one per `prebootSpecs` entry (absent: its `defaultSpec`). Otherwise, or when no such copy is ready, the sandbox boots as usual.

prebootSpecs.description: The sizes `preboot` applies to. Absent: `defaultSpec` only.

restricted.description: An internal test: only the accounts the operator listed, and admins, see it in this list or can create from it (a create by anyone else answers as for an unknown template). Sandboxes that exist keep working for their owners.

runtime.description: Software baked into the template, e.g. {"herdr":"0.9.3"}.

sizes.description: A pool template's sizes besides `defaultSpec` (`vcpus` and `memMiB`; the disks are `defaultSpec`'s). A create names one with `vcpus` and `memMiB`; leaving the size out gets `defaultSpec`.

staged.description: A new version on its way to the hosts: a create may name it with `templateVersion`. A create without one gets it only once no host holds the current latest version any more; the operator's promote makes it the latest.

TemplateGPUType.description: A GPU type a GPU template offers (`Template.gpuTypes`).

maxPerMachine.description: The largest GPU count a create may ask for.

memGiB.description: GPU memory per GPU in GiB.

sizes.description: The sizes a create may pick, per GPU: a sandbox with N GPUs gets N times the vCPUs and memory and the disk once. A create that names no size gets the first.

kernel.description: The guest kernel the sandbox is pinned to, `sha256:<hex>`; absent: the host's default.

UpdateMachineRequest.description: A body key that is none of these is refused with `400 unknown_field` (keys match case-insensitively). The retired lifetime timeout (`timeoutSeconds`, `onTimeout` or `timeout`, any value but null) is `400 unknown_field` naming `maxRunMinutes` and `autoSuspendAfterSeconds` instead (to an `instabox-cli/<version>` `User-Agent`, that the CLI is out of date and the commands `instabox max-run`, `auto-suspend` and `rm`), and nothing changes.

apply.description: `restart`: a running or paused sandbox whose change needs a stop is stopped, resized and started again by one `resize` operation (`202`); see the operation. Absent: such a change is `409`. Anything else is `400 bad_request`.

autoSuspendAfterSeconds.description: The plan's rule (`AutoSuspendAfterSeconds`): a paid sandbox takes 300-1800 in whole minutes, as sent, or 0 (off) where the plan allows always on; below 300, above 1800 or not a multiple of 60 is `400 bad_request`; the free sandbox takes only 1800 (else `403 spec_not_allowed`), and 0 without always on is `403 spec_not_allowed` too. A refused value leaves the setting unchanged; the reply shows the effective value. API keys follow the owner's policy. Separately, with manual lifecycle (`GET /v1/me`) or an admin sign-in session: 120-86400, or 0 (off). Absent: unchanged.

memMiB.description: New memory (MiB) of a stopped paid sandbox, as `vcpus`; 0 or absent: unchanged.

metadata.description: Replaces the metadata (same limits as `Metadata`); {} clears it; null or absent: unchanged.

name.description: New name, unique among the org's live sandboxes; 1-63 of a-z, 0-9, '-', starting with a letter or digit. Absent: unchanged.

persistentDiskGiB.description: New disk (`/data`) size in GiB, 1-1024, up to the plan's `maxDiskGiB`; 0 or absent: unchanged. Grow: a running box grows online (no restart, processes keep running); if it can't (rare: the box is unreachable or its host is older), `409 grow_needs_stop` (stop it and send the size again); a stopped box grows at its next start. Shrink: only while stopped (else `409 operation_conflict`), and only when the used data plus 10% (at least 1 GiB) fits; else `409 disk_too_small`, with the smallest size that fits in the message, and the box unchanged. Past 1024 is `400 bad_request`, and so is growing on a template without the `root-grow` capability (a shrink needs none); a free box's disk is fixed (`400 spec_not_allowed`, running or stopped). The Python SDK's `machines.resize(m, disk_gib)` sends this field.

rootDiskGiB.description: Admins only: new root filesystem size in GiB (the template sizes it). From anyone else it is `400 spec_not_allowed`; grow the disk with `persistentDiskGiB`.

vault.description: False disables legacy Vault delivery; true cannot re-enable the legacy flag; absent is unchanged. Org Secret selections are independent.

vcpus.description: New vCPUs of a stopped paid sandbox: with `memMiB`, one of the workspace's `allowedSpecs`, or of its template's `defaultSpec` and `sizes` when the template has a `pool` (alone: the one size with that many vCPUs); 0 or absent: unchanged. Applied at its next start (see the operation). Running is `409 operation_conflict` (stop it first), and so is paused (resume it, then stop it); another size, or the free sandbox, is `400 spec_not_allowed`.

directSecrets.description: Replaces the direct references in full; [] clears. Not sent together with envSecrets. Null is rejected.

envSecrets.description: Explicit env names; [] clears. Omission keeps the prior list. Null and all are rejected.

UpdateOrgBillingRequest.description: Give at least one of the fields.

overageAlert.description: Whether to email when usage goes beyond what the month includes.

spendCapUSD.description: The cap on this month's usage beyond the allowance; 0: nothing beyond it; -1: no cap.

usageAlertPercent.description: The usage alert's share of what the month includes; 0: off.

maxBytes.description: The largest body the URL takes (5 GiB).

url.description: PUT the file's raw bytes here; it carries its own credential.

allocatedDiskGiB.description: The `/data` of all your live sandboxes, in GiB: what `limits.maxStoredGiB` is checked against. Absent from older servers.

computedAt.description: When the byte figures were last computed or confirmed. A usage run every 10 minutes confirms unchanged orgs and recomputes changed ones (each at most every 30 minutes), so usually under an hour old. An org that stores nothing reads 0 as of now; null only while stored data waits for its first run.

cost.description: This calendar month's (UTC) cost in USD as the hourly rating priced it (`costUSD`, with `runtimeUSD`, `storageUSD` and `egressUSD`), up to `ratedUntil`; the allowance (`allowanceUSD`, `creditRemainingUSD`, `overageUSD`) and the credit balance (`creditsUSD`, `creditsExpireAt`). The same figures as `usage` on `GET /v1/orgs/{id}`. A free sandbox is never billed, so a free month is `0`. Absent from older servers.

exclusiveBytes.description: No longer computed: always 0. (Was the part of storedBytes no other org shares.)

logicalBytes.description: Full size of your sandboxes and snapshots.

org.description: The org these figures and limits describe: your personal org by default, a workspace key's workspace, or the one named with `org`. Absent from older servers.

storage.description: storedBytes by sandbox. Absent before your first measurement, and from older servers.

storedBytes.description: What they take up once compressed, with shared data counted once and the templates' own content (an unchanged root filesystem) not counted: what you wrote on the root filesystem counts. Paused sandboxes' saved memory does not count.

UsageLimits.description: Your limits. An admin may change maxMachines per user.

liveSnapshots.description: Snapshots of running sandboxes are allowed (some may still be refused until the server is fully updated). Absent: they are not.

machineSpec.description: The default size, what a create naming no size gets (4 vCPUs, 8 GiB memory by default; no rootDiskGiB: the template's). Absent from servers before fixed sizes.

machineSpecs.description: Every size your new sandboxes may have in your personal org, as `GET /v1/me` `allowedSpecs`: machineSpec first, then its plan's others (Pro: 2/4, 4/8, 8/16; Builder: 2/4 up to 16/32; Team and Enterprise: 2/4 up to 32/64) and any size an admin granted it. Pick one by naming its vcpus and memMiB on create.

maxMachines.description: Sandboxes in any state, checked on create (default 1). 0 with maxMachines in `unlimited`: no limit (a paid plan without one); 0 otherwise: none allowed. There are no vCPU or memory quotas.

maxStoredGiB.description: Stored data limit (default 200), checked against allocatedDiskGiB when you create a sandbox or snapshot. 0: no limit (listed in `unlimited`).

orgSecrets.description: Org Secret APIs are available alongside the per-user Vault. Absent or false: use Vault.

unlimited.description: The count limits above that do not apply. Each is still sent as 0 for older clients, but means no limit, not none allowed; a 0 not listed is a real 0 (a free org's maxMachines 0: no free sandboxes). Always an array from current servers (empty when every limit applies); absent or null from older ones, whose 0 is ambiguous. A 0 in a limit means unlimited when the limit's name is in this list.

vault.description: Vault limits per user; also used for org Secret quotas when orgSecrets is true.

diskBytes.description: Its saved disks' share of storedBytes: `/data` and what was written on the root filesystem (0 until its disks are first saved, on stop, pause or snapshot).

UsageStorage.description: storedBytes by sandbox, from the same measurement. Data that several of your sandboxes and snapshots share is split evenly between them, so the figures sum to storedBytes.

VaultApplied.description: One write of the Vault into a machine.

error.description: Why the write failed, when it did.

files.description: The files written (or, when the write failed, those of the last write, kept for the next reconciliation).

kept.description: Files that no longer apply but were left (changed in the machine since, or not writable).

removed.description: Files of an earlier write removed because they no longer apply.

sha256.description: Hex sha256 of the content written.

VaultItem.description: Per-user Vault metadata (docs/vault.md). Values are absent from lists.

machines.description: The caller's live machines the item applies to (selector matches, Vault not off).

migrationReason.description: Reason an item was retained for recovery.

name.description: Unique per user. An env item's name is the variable's name.

path.description: File items: the target, relative to the home directory.

selector.description: Historical labels; these do not control org Secret selection.

maxBytes.description: Raw bytes of all Secret values per org (server default 262144).

WakeMachineRequest.description: The optional body of `POST /v1/machines/{id}/wake`, which takes no fields; any key is refused with `400 unknown_field`.

disabledReason.description: Why the server disabled it: every attempt failed for 5 days. Absent when an admin did, or it is enabled.

failingSince.description: The first failed attempt since the last success.

secret.description: The signing secret (`whsec_` + base64 key), only in the responses of create and rotate.

response.description: The first KiB of the response body.

status.description: The response status; absent when there was no response.

retryable.description: Whether POST .../retry would queue this delivery now: false while it is pending, and once its event is too old to retry (409 operation_conflict otherwise).

WebhookEvent.description:
The body of every webhook request. Requests are signed per Standard
Webhooks: `webhook-id` (the event ID: deduplicate on it),
`webhook-timestamp` (Unix seconds) and `webhook-signature`
(`v1,<base64 HMAC-SHA256 of "<id>.<timestamp>.<body>">`, space
separated when two secrets sign).

data.description:
sandbox.*: `sandbox` {id, name, metadata}, `previousState`, `state`,
`reason` (user, idle, archive, wake, admin, system, ...),
`operationId`, and on sandbox.error `error`. snapshot.*: `snapshot`
{id, name, description, sourceSandboxId, status}, and on
snapshot.failed `error`.

maxEndpoints.description: How many endpoints the org may have (default 10).

apiKey.description:
API key (`ibk_...`) with scopes; also accepted as `Authorization: Bearer ibk_...`.
Accepted on sandbox, snapshot, operation, template and usage routes per scope
(see API keys), never on key management, sessions, logout or admin routes.
apiKey.name: X-API-Key

bearerAuth.description: Opaque instabox access token (1 hour). Refresh with `/v1/auth/refresh` (refresh token valid 30 days, rotates on use).

portAgent.description: Port ibpv_...; accepted only on this sandbox's port list, publish and unpublish routes, while it runs.
portAgent.name: Authorization

sessionCookie.description:
Dashboard browser session from `/auth/github/login` (7 days idle, 30 days at
most). Used only when no Authorization header is sent. Requests other than
GET and HEAD must send `X-Instabox-CSRF` (from `GET /v1/me`) and an `Origin`
equal to the server's `publicUrl`; otherwise `403 permission_denied`.
sessionCookie.name: instabox_session

info.description:
The instabox API creates and manages sandboxes: Linux computers in the
cloud that keep their files and software, for coding agents such as
Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode. It also issues short-lived SSH
credentials for reaching them. The `instabox` CLI, the dashboard, herdr,
cmux and Orca all use it. The Go types in `pkg/instaboxapi` are the
source of truth; this document mirrors them.

The API is older than the name "sandbox". Paths, fields and scopes call a
sandbox a machine (`/v1/machines`, `machineId`, `machines:read`), and
pausing is `suspend` and `resume`. The text here says "sandbox" and
"pause"; code keeps the API's names.

## Authentication

The base URL is `https://api.instabox.sh`. Programs and agents send an API
key: `X-API-Key: ibk_...` or `Authorization: Bearer ibk_...`, for example
`curl -H "X-API-Key: $INSTABOX_API_KEY" https://api.instabox.sh/v1/machines`.
Create one in the dashboard (API keys) or with `instabox keys create`; see
API keys below for scopes. A bad key gets a 401 whose `error.code` says
why: `missing_key`, `malformed_key`, `invalid_key`, `expired_key`,
`revoked_key`, or `session_expired` for a dashboard session, with a `hint`
and `docs` (https://instabox.sh/docs/api#authentication-errors). A key
without the scope a route needs gets `403 missing_scope`. Docs for agents:
https://instabox.sh/llms.txt.

## Sandboxes

- A new sandbox gets the default size, 4 vCPUs and 8 GiB of memory
  (`limits.machineSpec` in `GET /v1/usage`), unless `vcpus` and `memMiB`
  name another size of your plan (Pro: 2/4, 4/8, 8/16; Builder: 2/4 up to 16/32; Team and Enterprise: 2/4 up to 32/64) or one an admin granted the org; `GET /v1/me` `allowedSpecs`
  lists the personal org's, `GET /v1/orgs` each org's. Leave `persistentDiskGiB` and `rootDiskGiB` out at create:
  the disks come with the size, and a disk size other than the one the sandbox gets is `400 spec_not_allowed`.
  A paid sandbox's disk grows afterwards with `PATCH /v1/machines/{id}`
  `{"persistentDiskGiB": N}`: 1-1024 GiB; a running sandbox's disk grows live, a shrink
  applies while it is stopped, at its next boot (refused as `disk_too_small` when the data
  no longer fits), up to the plan's `maxDiskGiB` and the stored-data limit.
  Its vCPUs and memory move to another of the plan's sizes the same way
  (`{"vcpus": N, "memMiB": M}`, while it is stopped, applied at its next boot);
  a free sandbox's size is fixed.
- A sandbox has one **disk** (`/data`, which holds HOME at `/data/home`), 20 GiB
  by default, kept across stop, pause and start. The operating system and the
  template's software sit on a root filesystem the template sizes; only admins grow it
  (`rootDiskGiB`).
- A free org (every personal org) can have 1 sandbox in any state
  (stopped and paused ones count), 5 snapshots and 200 GiB of stored data
  across sandboxes and snapshots; Pro 500 sandboxes (100 running),
  Builder 1000 sandboxes (200 running), Team no sandbox limit (500 running).
  `GET /v1/usage` shows the current
  figures. An admin can change an org's sandbox limit.

## Conventions

- JSON bodies use camelCase. Times are RFC 3339 in UTC.
- All endpoints except `/v1/auth/device`, `/v1/auth/device/token`,
  `/v1/auth/cli/token`, `/v1/auth/refresh` and `/v1/openapi.json` require `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>`, or the
  dashboard's `instabox_session` cookie (see `sessionCookie`; mutations then need
  `X-Instabox-CSRF` and a same-origin `Origin`). Sandbox, snapshot and operation endpoints
  also accept an API key (see API keys).
- `/v1/admin/*` and `/metrics` (from outside `metrics.allowFrom`) are
  admin-only; other users get `403 permission_denied`.
- Access: GitHub and Google sign-in is public. A verified provider identity
  creates a regular user. With the server's invite gate on (`inviteRequired`
  in server.json or `INSTABOX_INVITE_REQUIRED=true`), a new account must then
  redeem an invite code (`POST /v1/invites/redeem`) before it may use anything
  but `GET /v1/me` and `POST /v1/auth/logout`: every other route answers
  `403 invite_required` until it does. `GET /v1/me` says whether the gate is
  on (`inviteRequired`) and whether the account passed it (`activated`);
  admins and accounts from before the gate always pass. Disabled users cannot
  sign in, refresh credentials, call authenticated APIs or connect over SSH.
  GitHub users keep their positive numeric IDs; Google users get distinct
  negative IDs assigned by instabox. Matching emails never link accounts.
- Every non-2xx response has the error envelope
  `{"error": {"code", "message", "requestId", "retryable", "operationId"}}`.
- Changes to a sandbox are asynchronous: they return `202 Accepted` with an
  `Operation`. Poll `GET /v1/operations/{id}?wait=25s` (a long poll) until
  `state` is `succeeded` or `failed`. Accepted does not mean ready.

## API keys

Programs, CI and agents use an API key (`ibk_...`) instead of signing in:
send `X-API-Key: ibk_...` (or `Authorization: Bearer ibk_...`; when
both are sent they must carry the same key, else `400 bad_request`). You
create keys while signed in (`POST /v1/keys`, API keys in the dashboard
sidebar, or `instabox keys create`); the secret is shown once and only its
sha256 is stored. Every key belongs to one org and reaches no other: `POST /v1/keys`
makes one of your personal org, `POST /v1/orgs/{id}/keys` one of any org you
manage (see Workspace API keys). A key expires after `expiresInDays` (1-365) or, without it, never; an org has at
most 20 active keys. An expired or revoked key gets `401 expired_key` or
`401 revoked_key`. Disabling a user revokes their keys, and every request
checks that the user is not disabled. SSH certificates a key
issued stop working when the key is revoked or expires.

A key carries scopes: read, write and delete for each resource. A route the
key's scopes do not cover returns `403 missing_scope`. A `:write` or
`:delete` scope includes the `:read` scope of the same resource. Signed-in
sessions have every scope.

- `machines:read`: `GET /v1/machines`, `GET /v1/machines/{id}`, `GET /v1/machines/{id}/connection-info`, `GET /v1/machines/{id}/metrics`, `GET /v1/machines/{id}/usage`, `GET /v1/operations/{id}`, `GET /v1/templates`, `GET /v1/usage`
- `machines:write`: `POST /v1/machines`, `PATCH /v1/machines/{id}` (name, idle pause, metadata), `POST /v1/machines/{id}/start`, `/stop`, `/suspend`, `/resume`, `/restore` (disks back to a snapshot's, in place), `POST /v1/machines/{id}/connections` (SSH certificates), `POST`, `DELETE /v1/machines/{id}/ssh-tokens` (SSH tokens), `POST /v1/machines/{id}/exec` (run a command)
- `machines:delete`: `DELETE /v1/machines/{id}`
- `images:read`: `GET /v1/snapshots`, `GET /v1/snapshots/{id}`, `GET /v1/snapshots/{id}/files`, `GET /v1/templates`, `GET /v1/usage`, `GET /v1/operations/{id}`
- `images:write`: `POST /v1/machines/{id}/snapshots`
- `images:delete`: `DELETE /v1/snapshots/{id}`

The snapshot scopes keep the names they had when snapshots were called
images (`images:*`), because existing keys store them.

Keys created before these scopes may still carry `machines:ssh` (SSH
certificates and connection info) or `machines:exec` (exec). Those keep
working on their routes, but new keys cannot be given them.

Any key may call `GET /v1/me`. Keys never work on
`/v1/keys` (a leaked key cannot create more keys), `/v1/sessions`,
`/v1/auth/logout`, `/v1/admin/*` or `/metrics`, and never carry admin
rights: `start` with `host` gets `403 permission_denied`, another user's
snapshot is `404` as for any other user, and resizing gets
`400 spec_not_allowed`.

## Workspace API keys

A workspace's owner and admins make keys that belong to the
workspace, not to them (`POST /v1/orgs/{id}/keys`, signed-in sessions
only). Without `scopes`, a workspace key carries the `workspace:admin` scope: it is an
admin of that one workspace on every key-capable route, including the
workspace's management routes (rename, members, invites, invite code,
Secrets), which other keys cannot use (`403 missing_scope`); with
`APIKeyScope`s it is limited to them. It
acts as the workspace's owner (`GET /v1/me` names the owner, without
their email, and `orgId`) yet reaches nothing outside the workspace:
other orgs, their sandboxes and snapshots are `404`, a create that names
no `orgId` goes in the workspace, and the sandboxes it creates have no
Vault (use org Secrets). Billing, the Vault routes and key management
stay with sessions; desktop links are the machine creator's, signed in
or with their personal key (for a machine of their personal workspace),
so a workspace key gets `403 permission_denied` there. It keeps working when the member who made it leaves; it stops
when it is revoked or expires, or the workspace is deleted or purged. A workspace
has at most 20 active keys.

## Idempotency

Mutating POST and DELETE requests require an `Idempotency-Key` header
(1-200 printable ASCII characters). Keys are scoped to (user, key), a
workspace API key's to its workspace:
- Same key with the same method, path and body hash returns the original
  response (status and body) without performing the request again.
- Same key with a different request returns `409 idempotency_conflict`.
- Records are kept for 7 days; after that the key may be reused.
Generate a fresh random key for each action and save it before sending,
so a retry after a timeout or crash reuses it.

## Sandbox lifecycle

- A sandbox runs at most one operation at a time. A different change
  while one is running returns `409 operation_conflict` with `operationId`.
  Repeating the same change returns the running operation.
- A change that is already in effect (for example `start` on a running
  sandbox) returns an operation that has already `succeeded`.
- Pause (`suspend`) keeps the sandbox's running programs, and resume brings
  them back. `start` on a paused sandbox resumes it. If its programs cannot
  be brought back, the sandbox boots fresh and `runtime.processesPreserved`
  is `false`. Files are kept either way.
- Stop shuts the sandbox down; running programs end, files are kept.
  `stop` on a paused sandbox returns `409 operation_conflict` ("resume it
  first, then stop it, or delete it").
- Creating an SSH certificate connection resumes a sandbox paused for
  idleness; other non-running sandboxes return `409 machine_not_running`.
- Use requests may resume a sandbox paused for idleness. Manual pause/stop
  and archive require an explicit start or resume.
- Sandboxes have no lifetime timeout: they pause when idle (below). An
  archive deadline reached while idle-paused requires an explicit resume
  afterwards.
- Pause when idle: a sandbox with `autoSuspendAfterSeconds` is paused
  through an ordinary `suspend` operation (`trigger: idle`) once it has
  reported no activity for that long (docs/idle-suspend.md); activity is
  checked about once a minute. Every new sandbox has it, 30 minutes, unless
  its create request gives another time or 0 (never). The setting stays: a
  later resume or start keeps it. Every template accepts it: one with the
  `activity` capability ships probes for its agents; on the others, terminal
  and CPU activity alone count. Real work (exec, files, terminal traffic and preview requests)
  and task activity leases also prevent idle suspension. Exec, files,
  terminal and SSH certificate requests resume sandboxes paused for
  idleness before proceeding (`trigger: request`). Manual pause/stop and
  archive are never automatically undone. Preview links remain
  offline until resumed. Status reads and keepalives do not record activity.
- `revision` increases with each accepted change. An operation's results
  are written only if the sandbox's revision still equals the operation's.
- Deleted sandboxes are not listed; `GET /v1/machines/{id}` returns
  `404 not_found` for them.

## Templates and snapshots

A sandbox starts from a template (`templateId`: software that ships with
instabox) or from a snapshot (`snapshotId`). A snapshot is a saved copy of
a sandbox's system files and storage; a sandbox created from it gets both.
A system-files-only snapshot (`rootOnly`, no `dataSizeBytes`) gives the new
sandbox empty storage. Memory and running programs are not saved. Saving
a snapshot of a stopped sandbox needs it fully saved (`storage.synced`),
and every snapshot needs a template with the `identity-reset` capability.
HOME is `/data/home`, so credentials kept there (gh, Claude, Codex, git,
SSH) are included in new snapshots. A snapshot belongs to its source
sandbox's org: every member of the org uses it. New snapshot IDs start with `sn_`; older ones with `im_`,
and stay valid.

Where the server allows live snapshots, you can also snapshot a running
sandbox: the request answers `202` with the snapshot in
`status: pending`. The sandbox's files are frozen for well under a
second while they are copied, then the copy uploads in the background
and the snapshot becomes `ready`, or `failed` with `error`.
Poll `GET /v1/snapshots/{id}`. Only a `ready` snapshot can be used. The
copy is like the state after a sudden power cut: data that programs had
not written to disk yet is not included.

## Deprecated aliases

Until 2026-10 snapshots were called images. These names keep working
and are marked `deprecated` here; replies to them carry a `Deprecation`
header (RFC 9745) and, for the routes, a `Link` to the successor
(`rel="successor-version"`):

- `POST /v1/machines/{id}/images`, `GET /v1/images`, `GET /v1/images/{id}`,
  `GET /v1/images/{id}/files`, `DELETE /v1/images/{id}`: the
  `/snapshots` routes. They reply in the old shape: `GET /v1/images`
  returns `{"images": [...]}`, and each snapshot also has
  `official: false`, `owned: true` and `preinstalled: []`.
- `imageId` in `POST /v1/machines`: `snapshotId` (both: they must be equal).
- `Machine.image`, `Usage.images` and `UsageLimits.maxImages`: sent with
  the same values as `snapshot`, `snapshots` and `maxSnapshots`.

Official images were removed: software ships in templates.

## SSH

Connect with `ssh -p <port> <machineId>@<host>`. Clients
authenticate with a user certificate from
`POST /v1/machines/{id}/connections` (principal = sandbox ID) and trust the
server with a known_hosts line
`@cert-authority [<host>]:<port> <hostTrust.publicKey>`.

Without a key or the instabox CLI, a plain ssh client logs in with an SSH
token from `POST /v1/machines/{id}/ssh-tokens` as its user name:
`ssh ibssh_…@<host>`, with `-p <port>` unless SSH is on port 22
(the reply's `command`). The token is accepted with the `none` method,
which OpenSSH tries first, and ssh asks once to confirm the server's host
key (`hostKeyFingerprint`). A token is a secret: it works for anyone who
has it until it expires, is revoked (`DELETE /v1/machines/{id}/ssh-tokens`)
or the sandbox is deleted. Supported:
sessions (pty, shell, exec, subsystem, env, signals) and local port
forwarding. Not supported in v1: agent forwarding, X11, remote forwarding.

mosh works through the same login: when a session runs `mosh-server new`,
the server opens a UDP port that relays to the sandbox's mosh-server and
puts it in the `MOSH CONNECT` line. The relay outlives the SSH session and
closes after a day without traffic, when the sandbox stops or is deleted,
or when the grant is revoked.
Connections are closed when the sandbox stops, pauses or is deleted.

## Exec

`POST /v1/machines/{id}/exec` runs one command without an SSH client: the
server logs in to the sandbox the way SSH does (user `dev`, HOME
`/data/home`), runs `bash -lc <cmd>` and returns its output and exit code
in the response. With `Accept: text/event-stream` the output is streamed
as the command writes it instead. Use SSH for interactive work.

get.description:
RFC 8252 loopback flow for CLIs and desktop apps. The client listens on
a loopback port, opens this URL in the browser and waits for one request
to its redirect URI. Invalid parameters get an HTML error page (no
redirect). Without `provider`, redirects to the dashboard's
`/dashboard/cli-authorize?request=...` with a signed request valid for
10 minutes. The browser confirms its existing Instabox account, or
signs in with GitHub or Google before confirming. Approval is an
explicit, CSRF-protected POST to `/v1/auth/cli/authorize`.
An explicit `provider` starts that provider's OAuth flow directly (on a server
whose default sign-in is WorkOS, its sign-in page, where the person picks).
On completion the browser returns to
`redirect_uri?code=<ibc_...>&state=<state>`, or on failure to
`redirect_uri?error=<error>&error_description=...&state=<state>` where
`error` is `access_denied` (cancelled or disabled), `server_error`, or, with
the invite gate on, `invite_required` (the account is not activated and no
`invite` was sent) or `invite_invalid` (the code cannot be redeemed; checked
before the provider opens, by the identity service's invites plugin when
Better Auth is configured), or `quota_exceeded` (too many invalid invite codes
from this client address in the past hour, as for `POST /v1/invites/redeem`;
the code is not checked). A redeemable `invite` is redeemed as the sign-in
completes. The client must check `state`, then call `POST /v1/auth/cli/token`
within 60 seconds.

parameters.description: An invite code (`K7R2QX`; older `482913` and `ibi_...` codes work too) for an account that is not activated yet (`instabox login --invite-code`).
parameters.name: invite

parameters.description: Optional explicit provider; omitted means confirm an account in the dashboard. `workos` signs in through WorkOS's page whenever WorkOS is configured, also while it is dark-launched (docs/workos.md).
parameters.name: provider

parameters.description: Exactly `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback` or `http://[::1]:<port>/callback`, port 1024-65535 (no `localhost`, query or fragment).
parameters.name: redirect_uri

parameters.description: Client CSRF value, 16-256 printable ASCII characters (no space), echoed to the redirect URI.

post.description:
The body is optional. The reply holds a `claimToken` (`ibg_...`), the agent's
secret for polling, and a `userCode` (`XXXX-XXXX`) with the dashboard's claim
page (`verificationUri`; `verificationUriComplete` has the code filled in).
The agent shows the person the page and the code and polls
`POST /v1/auth/agent/token` every `interval` seconds. The person opens the page
on any device, signs in or signs up with GitHub or Google, checks what the
agent asked for and approves; the agent's next poll collects an API key of
the person's personal org. Nothing exists before the claim: no account, no
key, no session.

`name` is the key's name (at most 64 bytes, default `agent`), `email` a hint
for the person who should claim (nothing is sent to it), `scopes` the
`APIKeyScope`s asked for (default `machines:read machines:write
machines:delete images:read`) and `expiresInDays` the key's life (0: never).
The person may approve fewer scopes or a shorter life. A code can be claimed
for 24 hours (`expiresIn`, `expiresAt`). At most 20 registrations per client
network per hour, counted across every control host (`429 quota_exceeded`
with `retryAfterSeconds`); a server without a dashboard
(`publicUrl`) answers `503`.

post.description:
Requires a sign-in session past the invite gate (an API key gets
`403 permission_denied`; the dashboard's cookie needs its `X-Instabox-CSRF`
token and a trusted Origin). `decision` is `approve` or `deny`. `scopes`
and `expiresInDays`, when sent, reduce what the agent asked for: a non-empty
subset of its scopes and a life no longer than it requested (a finite one
cannot become `0`); anything broader, or a scope outside `APIKeyScope`, is
`400`. Approval records the decision; the key
itself is made by the agent's next poll, so an agent that never comes back
gets no key. The agent then has at least an hour to collect it. An account
that already holds 20 active keys gets `429 quota_exceeded`. `userId`, when
sent, must be the session's account (`409 operation_conflict` otherwise).
A code no agent is waiting with is `404 not_found` and counts against the
claim limiter (see `GET`).

post.description:
Like the device flow's poll: `400 authorization_pending` until the person
decides, `slow_down` when polled faster than `interval` (the server added 5 seconds
to its interval; double yours to catch up from any gap),
`expired_token` once the code ran out or the registration is over (register
again), `access_denied` when the person refused or their account is gone
since. `authorization_pending` and `slow_down` carry `retryAfterSeconds` (and
`Retry-After`), the interval the server now expects: 5 seconds for the first
10 minutes of a registration, then 30, then 60 after an hour; poll no faster.

Once the person approved, the poll makes the API key, in the person's
personal org, with the scopes and expiry they approved, and returns it with
its secret. The registration is then delivered for 10 minutes: a poll with the
same `claimToken` returns the same key again (an answer lost on the way, or a
key the agent could not store, is recovered by polling again). It ends on the
key's first authenticated use on any route, on `{"claimToken", "ack": true}`
(send it once the key is stored; `204`, and again `204` if repeated), or at the
window's end, when a key neither used nor acknowledged is revoked and the poll
answers `expired_token` with `reason: key_revoked_unused`. The server keeps the
secret only sealed (AES-GCM) for that window. An `ack` before a key was
delivered is `400 bad_request`. A person whose account already holds 20
active keys gets the agent `429 quota_exceeded` until they revoke one
(retryable). An unknown `claimToken` is `400 bad_request`.

post.description: Returns a `create` operation whose `machineId` is the new sandbox. Start from a template (`templateId`) or one of your snapshots (`snapshotId`). A sandbox gets the default size (4 vCPUs, 8 GiB memory) when the size fields are left out. For another size of your plan (Pro: 2/4, 4/8, 8/16; Builder: 2/4 up to 16/32; Team and Enterprise: 2/4 up to 32/64) or one an admin granted the org (`GET /v1/orgs` `allowedSpecs` lists them), name its `vcpus` and `memMiB`. Any other size is refused with `400 spec_not_allowed`. The free plan creates from agent-browser, android, omarchy or ci only (`403 template_not_allowed`); a create from a snapshot is not limited, except a snapshot of an internal-test template (`restricted` in `GET /v1/templates`), which only the accounts allowed to create from the template (and whoever took the snapshot) may use (`403 template_not_allowed`). An internal-test template has a limit on its machines (`403 template_limit`); a template whose guest kernel no host has is `503 kernel_unavailable`, and one with no version on any host (during a template rollout) is `503 template_unavailable`. Counts toward your plan's sandbox limit (`429 quota_exceeded`). When no host has room, the operation fails with `no_capacity` (retryable); with `failFast` the create is refused at once instead (`503 no_capacity`, nothing created, no operation). Retry `no_capacity` with backoff (see `Unavailable`) or try another size or template. A create from a template or from a system-files-only snapshot that fails before it gets a host (`no_capacity`, or any other error at that point) has its sandbox deleted with the failure (GET returns 404), so it does not count toward your limit and its name is free to retry. A create from a snapshot with storage stays, `stopped`; start it later. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`.

A delete replaces an operation still `queued`: that operation fails with `operation_conflict`

patch.description:
Synchronous. Absent fields are unchanged. `autoSuspendAfterSeconds` and `metadata` apply in any state, also while an operation runs, and do not change `revision`: `metadata` replaces the metadata (`{}` clears it).
`name` renames the sandbox in any state, also while an operation runs. Its ID, public port URLs and SSH certificates stay the same; the old name stops resolving at once. A name another live sandbox of the org has is `409 operation_conflict`. The guest hostname (`instabox-<name>`) follows at the sandbox's next start or resume, `~/MACHINE.md` at its next start from stopped.
Resizing (`persistentDiskGiB`) grows a paid sandbox's disk (`/data`) up to the plan's `maxDiskGiB` (pro 200, builder 500, team and enterprise 1024) and the stored-data limit, and the org must be under that limit (`429 quota_exceeded`). A free sandbox's size is fixed (`400 spec_not_allowed`). An admin can override that per user (`diskResize`) and, from a signed-in session, grow any sandbox without the limit. Each size is 1-1024 GiB (more is `400 bad_request`), and needs no operation in progress (else `409 operation_conflict`). The disk (`/data`) of a running sandbox grows online: no restart, files and processes stay; when it can't (rare: the sandbox is unreachable or its host is older) it is `409 grow_needs_stop`: stop it and send the size again. A stopped sandbox's disk grows at its next start. It shrinks only while stopped (else `409 operation_conflict`) and only when the used data plus 10% (at least 1 GiB) fits (else `409 disk_too_small`, nothing changes); the shrink applies at the next start, which keeps the larger size if the data has grown past it by then. The system disk (`rootDiskGiB`, admins) only grows (a smaller size is `400 bad_request`), and only while stopped. Growing either disk needs a template with the `root-grow` capability (else `400 bad_request`); a shrink does not. At create the disks come with the size; this is the way to get bigger ones.
`vcpus` and `memMiB` change a paid sandbox's size to another of its workspace's sizes (`allowedSpecs` of `GET /v1/orgs/{id}`), named as at create: one field picks the one size that matches it, else name both. The sandbox must be stopped with no operation in progress (else `409 operation_conflict`); the new size applies at its next start, which boots it fresh (files stay), and running time is rated at the new size from then on. That start's operation fails, and the sandbox stays stopped at its new size, when its host has no room for the new size (`no_capacity`) or runs an older node-agent that cannot resize (`host_unavailable`), both retryable; resize it back or start it later. A size the plan does not offer and the free sandbox are `400 spec_not_allowed` in any state (checked before the 409); the same size changes nothing. Admins may give any size within the API's ranges. As at create, a field it does not know is `400 unknown_field` and nothing changes, so `diskGiB` here is refused.
`apply: "restart"` lets a running or paused sandbox take a change that needs a stop (`vcpus`/`memMiB`, a `/data` shrink, a system-disk grow, or a grow it can't do online) instead of the `409`: the reply is `202` with one `resize` operation, under this request's idempotency key, that stops it (resuming a paused one first; its running processes end), applies the size and starts it again (phases `stopping`, `resizing`, `booting`). The server finishes it even if the caller goes away, so a sandbox can resize itself. When it can't start at the new size, it starts again at the old one and the operation fails with the reason. A change it can take as it is (a stopped sandbox, an online grow) is the usual `200`. `GET /v1/me` `resizeRestart` says the server takes it; a server that does not yet answers `400 resize_restart_off`. It is checked against the settings this request leaves: `maxRunMinutes: 0` with it is `400 max_run_disabled` (resize, then set it). The operation boots under the max-run it was accepted with. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`.

post.description: A graphical desktop in the machine: Xvfb, an Xfce session, Chromium and a VNC server, which GET /v1/machines/{id}/vnc reaches once it runs. Nothing runs until asked for. The agent-browser, android, herdr and orca templates include the packages; universal and t3 do not. `status` (the default) reports the state; `install` starts installing the packages in the background (about half a minute, about 1.4 GiB of the root disk) and returns at once; `start` starts the desktop of an installed machine and waits for its VNC server. `start` never installs: on a machine without the packages it starts nothing and returns the state with `installed` false and a `hint` saying what to send next. There, send `install`, poll `status` until `installed` is true, then `start`. `width` and `height` size the screen of a desktop that `start` starts (default 1280x800, within 800-2560 x 600-1600). The packages stay installed, and snapshots keep them. `takeover` gives the caller control of the desktop (`controller: human`, `yours: true`): the computer-use MCP in the machine refuses input tools until `handback` returns it to the agent. Control is held per sign-in session (or API key): every call the holder makes renews it, and it returns to the agent 30 s after the holder's last call (a closed viewer), while the same session finds it again after a reload. `handback` by anyone else changes nothing; `takeover` by anyone else takes it over. The lock is advisory: tools driving the display directly (xdotool) do not consult it. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

delete.description: Every link minted for this machine so far stops working, and the sessions open through them end within about 3 seconds (each checks every 3 s, on any server instance), or immediately if the check can't be completed. Links minted afterwards work. Only the machine's creator, signed in or with their personal key, revokes its links: another member of its org, or a workspace API key, gets 403 `permission_denied`, and opens the desktop itself over GET /v1/machines/{id}/vnc (which needs `machines:write`); 404 means the caller cannot reach the machine. A personal key reaches only the machines of its owner's personal workspace. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

post.description: Returns a link to the dashboard's full-screen desktop viewer, which anyone with the link can open, or embed in an iframe, without signing in. Expiry stops new connections; revoke ends open sessions: a session opened before `expiresAt` goes on until the viewer leaves, DELETE on this path revokes the link, or the machine or account is deleted. The token in its fragment is signed by the server and binds this machine, its owner and the link's mode; it is not an API key. View-only (the default): the server drops the viewer's input. The machine and its desktop must be running when the link is opened (GET /v1/machines/{id}/vnc rules), not when it is made: the link comes back at once. Only the machine's creator, signed in or with their personal key, makes and revokes its links: another member of its org, or a workspace API key, gets 403 `permission_denied`, and opens the desktop itself over GET /v1/machines/{id}/vnc (which needs `machines:write`); 404 means the caller cannot reach the machine. A personal key reaches only the machines of its owner's personal workspace. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

Runs the checks GET /v1/machines/{id}/vnc runs for a new connection and always answers 200 with `state`: `ok`; `expired` (expiry stops new connections); `revoked` (DELETE /v1/machines/{id}/desktop/stream ended it); `invalid` (anything else: not a link for this machine, or its owner's account is gone).

get.description: Server-sent events (`text/event-stream`) for the caller's open desktop session on the machine (GET /v1/machines/{id}/vnc): while that session is open the server runs the desktop's status every 3 s on a guest connection of the heartbeat's own (never the session's), with the caller as the control's owner (the heartbeat that keeps a control the caller holds, which lapses 30 s after the session closes), and sends each result as a `status` event whose data is a Desktop object (the latest one first); a beat the guest did not answer is a `stale` event whose data is `{"message": "..."}` (the status is stale until the next `status`), and `end` comes when the caller's last desktop session on the machine closes (its sessions, such as two tabs, share one stream of events). A comment line every 15 s keeps the connection alive. 404 `not_found` without an open desktop session of the caller's on the machine: poll POST /v1/machines/{id}/desktop instead. 429 `quota_exceeded` beyond 8 open streams per desktop session. A browser session is checked for the dashboard's origin: an `Origin` header, when the browser sends one (cross-origin), must be the dashboard's; without one (a same-origin `EventSource` carries none) the request is refused only when `Sec-Fetch-Site` or `Referer` says it comes from elsewhere. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

get.description: Read inside the sandbox now (`df` as its user, over the same path as exec): used, available and size in bytes and the inode use of `/data` (the disk, what `PATCH /v1/machines/{id}` with `persistentDiskGiB` grows) and `/` (the root filesystem). Each filesystem has a level: `ok` below 80%, `high` from 80%, `critical` from 90%, `full` at 100% or with no inodes left; `warning` is set from 90%. It never wakes a paused sandbox and does not count as activity: a sandbox that is not running is a 409 `machine_not_running`. API keys: needs the scope `machines:read`.
get.summary: How full the running sandbox's disks are (/data and /), with a near-full warning.

post.description:
Runs `cmd` with `bash -lc` as the sandbox's login user (`dev`, HOME
`/data/home`, the user SSH sessions get), after exporting `envs` and
changing to `cwd` (default HOME, even if the profile changes directory;
a `cwd` that does not exist makes the command fail with exit code 1). `stdin` is fed to the command, then EOF:
UTF-8 text of at most 1 MiB (1048576 bytes, not characters); bytes that
are not UTF-8 become U+FFFD, so base64-encode binary input or write it
with `PUT /v1/machines/{id}/files` first (see `ExecRequest.stdin`).

Instead of `cmd`, send `argv` (a program and its arguments) to run
it with no shell: `{"argv": ["printf", "%s|", "a b", "$X"]}` prints
`a b|$X|`. The login profile, `envs` and `cwd` apply the same way;
only the parsing of the command differs. Set exactly one of `cmd`
and `argv`.

The request blocks until the command exits or `timeoutSeconds` passes.
On timeout the command's process group is killed (SIGKILL) and the
result has `timedOut: true` and `exitCode: 124` (also when the sandbox
did not start the command in time). A command killed by a signal has
`signal` set and `exitCode` 128+N for standard signal N, otherwise
255. A non-zero exit code is a `200` result,
not an error. The request returns when the command exits, even if
a process it started in the background keeps its stdout or stderr
open: that process keeps running, output it writes later than about
a second after the exit is not returned, and its later writes to
that output fail with a broken pipe, so redirect a server's stdout
and stderr to a file (`nohup server >log 2>&1 &`). stdout and stderr
keep their first 1 MiB each (`truncated: true` when either was cut);
invalid UTF-8 is replaced with U+FFFD (`invalidUtf8: true`), so binary
output is not byte-exact: read files with
`GET /v1/machines/{id}/files/content`.

The sandbox must be `running` (`409 machine_not_running`). At most 32
requests run at once per user on the free plan, per workspace for a
workspace's API keys (Pro 64; Builder, Team
and Enterprise 256), across all your sandboxes. Commands,
file reads, desktop, port-forward and Secret refresh calls share this
limit. A background command counts only while it starts. More get a
retryable `429 quota_exceeded` (server config `limits.maxExecsPerUser`,
`plans.<tier>.maxExecs` and `limits.maxExecsPerOrg`,
not reported by `GET /v1/usage`). If the sandbox cannot be reached,
`503 host_unavailable`; when the connection is lost after the command
started it is not `retryable`, since the command may have run (it is
killed, not left running). An API server that restarts mid-command
kills it and answers a `retryable` `503 host_unavailable` ("the API
server restarted before the command finished").
Not idempotent: no Idempotency-Key, and a retry runs the command again.
API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

Streaming: send `Accept: text/event-stream` to get the output as the
command writes it, as server-sent events: a `stdout` or `stderr`
event (data: `ExecOutput`) for each chunk, a `: ping` comment every
15 s while the command is quiet, then one `exit` event (data: the
`ExecResult`, with empty `stdout` and `stderr` and never
`truncated`: streamed output is not capped) or `error` event (data:
an `ErrorBody`, e.g. `host_unavailable` when the connection to the
sandbox was lost). Errors found before the command starts (`400`,
`404`, `409`, `429`, a `503` dial failure) are plain JSON responses.
Closing the stream kills the command. Timeouts are the same as
without streaming; for a command longer than 10 minutes start it
in the background (`instabox exec --background`) and follow its log.

200.description: The command ran (whatever its exit code).

get.description: Lists a directory or returns a file of a running sandbox you own, read live the same way exec runs commands, as root (sudo; as the dev user if sudo needs a password). The response is the Files shape: a directory lists its entries (directories first, then by name, at most 5000); a regular file returns its content as text (at most 256 KiB) unless it is binary. Symbolic links in the path are followed. A sandbox paused for idleness is resumed first; other non-running sandboxes return 409 `machine_not_running`. A path that does not exist is 404. It counts toward the per-user limit of requests at once (free plan 32; Pro 64; Builder, Team and Enterprise 256). API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

parameters.name: path

get.summary: Read a file or directory of a running sandbox.

put.description: Streams the raw request body into the file at `path` of a running sandbox, as the sandbox's user (like exec; no sudo). Any bytes, up to 5 GiB (5368709120 bytes; more is 413 `too_large`); there is no exec body or output cap on this route. The body goes to a temporary file in the destination's directory, which is renamed over `path` only once every byte arrived, so a failed or interrupted upload never leaves a partial file. A transfer is cut off after 2 hours (7200 seconds; 408 `bad_request`) however steadily it moves. An existing file keeps its mode unless `mode` is given; a new one gets 0644. A symbolic link at `path` is followed. A missing parent directory is 404 `missing_parent` unless `parents=true`; a directory the user cannot write, or an existing file it cannot write, is 403 `permission_denied`; `path` naming a directory (or a parent that is a file) is 409 `not_a_file`; a full disk is 507 `no_space`. A sandbox paused for idleness is resumed first; other non-running sandboxes return 409 `machine_not_running`. An upload that moves no bytes for 60 seconds is dropped. With `token` (from POST /v1/machines/{id}/files/upload-url) the request needs no other credential, and `mode` and `parents` come from the token. It counts toward the per-user limit of requests at once (free plan 32; Pro 64; Builder, Team and Enterprise 256). API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

parameters.name: path

parameters.name: mode

parameters.description: Create missing parent directories (mkdir -p).
parameters.name: parents

parameters.description: An upload URL's signed token; replaces the credential.
parameters.name: token

507.description: The sandbox's disk filled during the write (`no_space`).

put.summary: Write (upload) a file to a running sandbox.

get.description: Streams the file at `path` of a running sandbox as `application/octet-stream` with its exact `Content-Length`, any size, read as root when the sandbox's sudo allows it, as its user otherwise (like the listing). The resolved path and octal mode are in the `X-Instabox-File-Path` (percent-encoded) and `X-Instabox-File-Mode` headers. A missing file is 404 `not_found`, a directory 409 `not_a_file`, an unreadable file 403 `permission_denied`; non-running sandboxes return 409 `machine_not_running`. A download that moves no bytes for 60 seconds is dropped, and any download is cut off after 2 hours. It counts toward the per-user limit of requests at once (free plan 32; Pro 64; Builder, Team and Enterprise 256). A cut download continues where it stopped: the response has `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and an `ETag` naming this version of the file (its size, inode, and modification and change times to the nanosecond), and a `Range: bytes=START-` or `bytes=START-END` header gets 206 with that part and a `Content-Range`. Send `If-Range` with the ETag so a file that changed since, even rewritten in place at the same size, comes back whole (200) instead of in a part of another version. A file whose times have no sub-second part gets no `ETag`, so `If-Range` always gets it whole. Any other `Range` (a suffix, several ranges) gets the whole file; a range that starts past the end is 416. `instabox cp` and `pull` resume this way and check the result against the file's sha256. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

parameters.name: path

parameters.description: One range with a first byte: `bytes=START-` or `bytes=START-END`.
parameters.name: Range

parameters.name: If-Range

ETag.description: This version of the file, for If-Range.

416.description: The range starts past the end of the file (`bad_request`); `Content-Range: bytes */SIZE` gives its size.

post.description: Returns a URL on the API's own origin that takes `PUT` of the file's raw bytes to `path` (PUT /v1/machines/{id}/files with a signed `token`) with no other credential, until `expiresAt`: by default 15 minutes, at most 1 hour. Hand it to a tool that should not hold your API key, or use it for a long upload. The token is HMAC-signed and binds the sandbox, `path`, `mode` and `parents`; it may be used more than once until it expires. Each upload still acts as you: it fails once your account is gone, or the API key that made the URL is revoked or expired, or you lose access to the sandbox (org membership is checked on every upload). The sandbox need not be running to create a URL; the upload has the PUT route's limits and errors (5 GiB). API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

post.description: Creates a new sandbox with copies of a running or stopped sandbox's system files and storage (`/data`, HOME included). The node-agent clones the disks copy-on-write on the source's host (a running source's files are frozen for a moment, as for a live snapshot) and cold boots the copy: no snapshot is saved, uploaded or downloaded, and none counts toward the snapshot limit. Memory and running programs are not copied. `{id}` is the source's ID or name. The answer is the create operation (`machineId` is the new sandbox); the fork is a create for every limit (starts a minute, concurrency, storage). It carries metadata `instabox-fork-of` = the source's ID. It keeps the source's idle auto-suspend, max run, metadata and delete deadline (the same instant) unless the request sets `autoSuspendAfterSeconds`, `maxRunMinutes`, `metadata` or `deleteAfterSeconds`; inherited values are checked against the plan exactly as a create's, and a refusal of one says it came from the source. It takes the source's org Secrets selection (proxy and direct references, by name; values are resolved again for the fork) unless the request names its own `secrets`, `envSecrets` or `directSecrets`. `409 fork_unavailable` (nothing created): the source is suspended or has no host, or its host cannot fork; save a snapshot and create from it instead. A fork is made only on its source's host: when that host is under maintenance or full, the request (or the operation) is `409 fork_unavailable`, retryable with Retry-After, `reason` `source_host_unavailable` or `source_host_full`; stop and start the source to move it, or save a snapshot and create from it. A source stopped moments ago may still be uploading its disks in the background: the request waits for that upload (as snapshot save does); one still running after that is `409 operation_conflict`, retryable, with Retry-After (nothing created). The same conflict fails the operation when the source's host is still busy with it when the fork is copied; that fork is then deleted. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`.
post.summary: Create a copy of a sandbox on its host, without a snapshot.

Every `POST /v1/machines/{id}/exec` that reached the sandbox (by any
account or tool; `noHistory` requests excepted) is recorded with
its exit code and the first 64 KiB of each output stream, so the
history answers while the sandbox runs, after it stopped or paused,
and across restarts; it is deleted with the sandbox. The server
keeps the newest 200 commands per sandbox. `limit` (default 50, at
most 200) and `cursor` (a previous page's `nextCursor`) page
through them. The output itself is in
`GET /v1/machines/{id}/history/{execId}`.
API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

get.description: `console` is the end of the sandbox's serial console: kernel and systemd boot messages, anything written to /dev/console, and errors from the VM monitor. It is kept on the sandbox's host across stops, pauses and restarts, to the last 8 MiB. `operations` are its last 20 operations (create, start, stop, pause, resume and delete, with their errors), oldest first. Reading the log never wakes the sandbox, and it works in every state. When the console cannot be read (the sandbox's disks are in storage, or its host is not answering), the response is still 200 with `consoleUnavailable` and the operations. To follow the log, pass the response's `cursor` as `after` on the next request: you get only the output written since (`instabox logs --follow`). Commands' own output is not here: it is kept with each background job, and the guest's full journal is `journalctl -b` over exec. API keys: needs the scope `machines:read`, so a read-only key can read the console output (the kernel command line and console carry no credentials; Secrets go through the secret proxy).

Only kills of `bootId`, the boot the job ran in, are returned (scope names repeat after a restart). A cgroup that is not a session scope, or no `bootId`, is a 400; a sandbox that is not running is a 409 `machine_not_running`. A claim counts toward the concurrent exec limit: a 429 `quota_exceeded` (retryable) when the user's execs are all in use. API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec`.

Returns a single-use tunnel endpoint (valid 60 s), an assertion the
runtime verifies against its trust file (valid 5 min, `aud` =
`orca:<machineId>`), and the runtime's E2EE public key. Every call
mints a new ticket, so it takes no `Idempotency-Key`; clients call it
once per socket. The first call after each sandbox change writes the
trust file into the sandbox. Never starts a sandbox: `409
machine_not_running`; a template without the `orca` capability: `409
orca_unsupported`; a runtime that is not up yet: `409
runtime_not_ready` (retryable).

post.description:
API keys require `machines:write`. Also accepts the sandbox-local port credential.
With `access` omitted or `public`, anyone with the returned URL can reach the whole
service on that port. With `access: private` the URL answers only requests that carry
the port's token: the `tokenUrl` of this response (the URL with `?_token=`, which a
browser opens once; the proxy redirects it to the URL without the token and sets the
`__Host-instabox_port_auth` cookie), that cookie, or `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
Other requests get 401 (403 for a wrong `_token`) without waking the sandbox. The
token is returned only by the publish that created or rotated it; the server keeps
its hash. The URL stays until the port is unpublished and answers only while the
sandbox runs; stopped or paused, it returns 503. Publishing a published port again
keeps its URL and sets its name when given; `access` changes who can reach it and
`rotateToken` (private ports) replaces the token, both closing the connections that
used the old access, like an unpublish. Publishing does not start a server on the
port. At most 16 ports per sandbox.

get.description:
On a running sandbox (or one that paused itself, which wakes as for
exec) the server runs `ps -e -ww -o pid=,ppid=,user:64=,pcpu=,pmem=,etimes=,args=`
through exec, stores the list and returns it with `live: true`. The
listing counts as an exec (the concurrency limit, the activity
lease) but is not in the history. On a stopped or paused sandbox it
returns the list stored last (`live: false`, `capturedAt`,
`trigger`): the server reads the processes just before it stops or
pauses a running sandbox (best effort: 5 seconds for the listing,
then its write, before the stop goes on), so the list is from the
moment of the stop and is there once the sandbox is stopped, and
`404 not_found` when none was ever read. Without `all=true`, kernel threads and the
listing's own processes (its shell, `ps`, `head` and the sshd
sessions exec runs it in) are left out. `truncated` says the
listing was cut at its last whole line (about 900 KB).
`503 host_unavailable` when a running sandbox cannot be reached;
`502 host_unavailable` when `ps` itself failed in it.
API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`, `machines:exec` (legacy).

post.description: Replaces the sandbox's root disk and `/data` with snapshot `snapshotId`'s (absent: the snapshot the sandbox was created from, else `400`). The sandbox keeps its ID, name, hostname, public port URLs and SSH configuration; everything on its disks since the snapshot is gone, including running programs. Its SSH host keys are new afterwards. The reply is a `restore` operation: a running sandbox is stopped first, the snapshot's disks are put on its host, and it boots them unless `desiredState` is `stopped`. Works on a running, stopped, paused or failed sandbox; `409 operation_conflict` while another operation runs, while a stopped sandbox's last changes are still uploading (retry). A snapshot in another host pool is refused (`409 spec_not_allowed`), as is one saved root-only, or whose `/data` is larger than the sandbox's disk (`400`, `409 spec_not_allowed`: grow the disk first). Booting the restored sandbox counts as a start for the plan's start limit and needs what a start needs (`402`, `429`). A server whose operator has not turned restores on yet answers `400 feature_disabled`; a sandbox whose host runs a node-agent that cannot restore in place `409 restore_unavailable` (nothing changed). API keys: needs one of the scopes `machines:write`.
